overview: Hanover was a German electorate whose ruler also became king of Great Britain in 1714. The territories remained separate states. Hanover became a kingdom in 1814 and was annexed by Prussia in 1866, so the imported map’s later endpoint does not represent continued Hanoverian independence.

periods.title: Electorate and personal union
periods.summary: The Hanoverian dynasty held the British crown while governing a separate German territory.

periods.title: Kingdom linked by its monarch
periods.summary: Hanover became a kingdom in 1814; the personal union lasted until 1837.

periods.title: A separate royal line
periods.summary: Ernst August’s accession ended the British personal union; Prussia annexed the kingdom in 1866.

items.text: Herrenhausen’s great fountain required a waterworks, not just an impressive stone basin. Engineers used the River Leine to drive machinery that forced water toward the garden. By 1720 the jet reached roughly thirty-five metres: royal spectacle depended on practical engineering.

The garden’s water system also needed extensive digging. Soldiers worked on the canal surrounding the Great Garden, while the machinery building stood on piles. Behind the elegant view were earthworks, structural supports and a great deal of labor.

The Herrenhausen orangery was built in 1723 as winter shelter for plants grown in pots. Gardening therefore included moving and protecting living collections season by season. An orangery was a serious piece of plant-care infrastructure, not simply a decorative room with a citrus name.

Göttingen’s university opened in 1737 and became an important center of research and teaching. Its history later included mathematician Carl Friedrich Gauss. The institution gives this small German kingdom a place in the history of science beyond the royal family.

In May 1833 Gauss and Wilhelm Weber successfully tested an electromagnetic telegraph in Göttingen. A wire more than a kilometre long linked the physics collection with the observatory, crossing the town’s roofs and towers. Electricity could now carry signals between working scientists.

Their apparatus was an early working telegraph, not the internet in miniature. Its importance lay in turning electrical effects into a usable signaling experiment over a real distance. Later systems developed the idea further; several inventors contributed to telegraphy.

Göttingen’s maternity institution offered lodging, food and care to women who were often unmarried. Directors’ diaries from the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries preserve their experiences. This is unusually direct evidence for pregnancy and birth among people largely absent from royal portraits.

The arrangement came with obligations: patients performed light work such as spinning or weaving and became subjects for clinical instruction. Assistance and unequal power existed together. Describing the institution simply as free healthcare would hide the demands placed on women and their babies.

The 1824 boundary treaty with the Netherlands dealt with markers, ditches and drainage as well as lines on a map. One surviving archival map records the arrangements around the Twist area. Borders could alter the management of shared land and water used by rural communities.

In 1837 King Ernst August rejected Hanover’s 1833 constitution. Seven Göttingen professors protested, including Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm, better known for collecting stories. Their stand cost all seven their jobs; three were also ordered out of the kingdom.

The protest was about an oath and the limits of royal authority, not just a disagreement between a king and some famous authors. University teaching existed inside a political system that could dismiss its scholars. The episode made academic independence a very practical problem.

German, Hanover’s constitution of 26 September 1833, section 3: “Die Regierungsform des Königreiches ist die erblich-monarchische.” Translation: “The kingdom’s form of government is hereditary monarchy.” The same constitution prescribed limits and obligations; four years later its revocation provoked the Göttingen professors’ protest.

ending.text: Prussia annexed Hanover in 1866, ending its independent kingdom. Its territory became a Prussian province, while towns, universities and local communities continued. The map’s coverage extending to 1878 must not be read as a surviving sovereign Hanoverian state.
